Response to Reviewer #2
(Note: Reviewer comments in black and our point-to-point replies in blue)
The current manuscript describes results from an analysis of satellite data regarding
impacts of extreme events (heat waves & cold spells) in the Southern Ocean. The
analysis reveals some interesting patterns and temporal trends, but there are major
weakness that compromise the integrity of the work and the robustness of the
conclusions. Below are specific comments beginning with major issues and followed
by minor comments.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful evaluation of our manuscript and
for highlighting both the strengths and areas requiring improvement. We appreciate
your acknowledgment of the novel spatial and temporal patterns identified in our
analysis. At the same time, we take seriously your concerns regarding the
methodological rigor and robustness of the conclusions. In response, we have carefully
addressed each of your specific comments and have made substantial revisions to the
manuscript to enhance its scientific integrity, clarity, and overall impact. These changes
include refining the methodological descriptions, improving dataset consistency,
clarifying the use of region-specific algorithms, strengthening model validation,
and updating our interpretation of key results. We believe these revisions have significantly
improved the quality and robustness of the study. A detailed point-by-point response to
each of your comments follows below.
Major Issues
1) All analyses regarding phytoplankton size classes and size distributions reported in
this study are not robust. The primary issue is that the authors are using global
relationships from previous publications and applying them to interpretations of
anomalies. For example, the phytoplankton size structure model of Sun et al. (2023) is
based on a global field data set (see their figure 1) where model performance is
evaluated over property values spanning multiple orders of magnitude (see their figure
3). It is clear in their figure 3 that even when plotted on log-log axes, there is significant
unexplained variance. If this model is then applied to Southern Ocean only data for
relatively small anomalies in SST and chlorophyll, there is no reason to believe that the
modeled predictions in phytoplankton size classes are robust. A similar issue also holds
for the Waga et al. (2019) model on phytoplankton size structure (or what the current
authors refer to as the chlorophyll size distribution, CSD). The Waga et al. paper is
focused on the impact of mesoscale eddies on CSD and is not inherently equally valid
for large scale impacts of extreme events. Waga et al. evaluated their model
performance based on, primarily, northern hemisphere data on the western edge of the
pacific ocean (see their figure 1), with limited data from the Southern Ocean with
undefined seasonal representation (and with roughly half of the data collected
immediately next to the Antarctic continent). The model used information on both
chlorophyll and spectral absorption, with the latter property included to aid in
retrievals in oligotrophic waters (essentially irrelevant for the current analysis. Waga et al.’s
resultant model was validated by comparing in situ CSD slopes to predicted slopes for
a dynamic range in values from ~0.5 to 3 (see their figure 2), an analysis the exhibited
significant unexplained variance. For the current study, reported anomalies in CSDs
associated with extreme events appear to largely fall within the range of +/- 0.1, which
certainly can not be considered significant (or even robust in sign) given the Waga et al
evaluation of model performance. Given the above considerations, I do not believe the
evaluation of community composition impacts of extreme events presented in the current
manuscript are robust and recommend that these be removed in future versions of this paper.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this critical and thoughtful assessment. We fully
acknowledge the concern regarding the limitations of applying globally derived
models—particularly those with substantial unexplained variance—to evaluate
relatively small anomalies in phytoplankton size structure, especially in a region as
optically and ecologically unique as the Southern Ocean. To address your concerns, we
have removed all analyses and results related to the chlorophyll size distribution (CSD)
model (Waga et al., 2019) from the manuscript. We agree that, given the limited
Southern Ocean validation and the narrow range of observed CSD anomalies (±0.1),
this metric does not provide a robust or interpretable signal in the context of extreme
events. Regarding the PSC model, we retained the PSC model of Sun et al. (2023) in
the revised manuscript, with important caveats and enhancements. We agree that the
original model was trained on global datasets and its application to Southern Ocean
anomalies requires validation. To this end, we conducted an independent evaluation
using a large in situ HPLC dataset (n = 3508 samples) from the Southern Ocean
spanning 1998–2023. Our analysis shows good agreement between model-predicted
and pigment-derived size class fractions (see revised Supplementary Figures 3 and 4),
indicating that the PSC model captures the dominant spatial and seasonal patterns of
phytoplankton community structure in this region. While we recognize that the PSC
model does not explicitly resolve short-term ecological dynamics such as grazing,
mixing history, or physiological acclimation, it provides a first-order estimate of
community shifts based on Chl-a and SST anomalies. We have now clarified these
limitations in the Discussion and Methods sections, and we emphasize that our
interpretations are qualitative and pattern-oriented rather than absolute.
2) (lines 182-236) I found this discussion of mechanisms for phytoplankton responses
inconsistent and not adequately supported. Here are specific examples:
a. (line 189-191) Here it is stated that phytoplankton in the SAZ are iron limited, but
then it says that MHWs alleviate light limitation and stimulate growth. First issue is
that there is no evidence provided that MHWs alleviate light limitation. Second, there
is no connection made between an increase in light and how that stimulates iron limited
phytoplankton.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that the original explanation
was incomplete and insufficiently supported. In the revised manuscript, we have
substantially rewritten this section to clarify the proposed mechanism:
(1) Light availability during MHWs. We now explicitly state that marine heatwaves
tend to enhance stratification and shoal the mixed layer, which increases the average
light exposure for phytoplankton—particularly in high-latitude regions where deep
mixing often limits irradiance.
(2) Interaction with iron limitation. We have clarified that MHWs alone do not directly
alleviate iron limitation in the SAZ. However, in regions with episodic or background
iron enrichment (e.g., via upwelling or dust deposition), the combination of increased
light and partial iron availability may support enhanced phytoplankton growth. We have
removed any implication of a direct causal link between MHWs and iron supply, and
instead frame the response as context-dependent.
b. (lines 191 -195) Here is it stated that in the AZ phytoplankton are co-limited by iron
and light, but no evidence is provided that this is always the case. More likely, the cells
are limited by light only in winter months, noting here that many MHWs for the AZ
occur in fall and winter (figure 1g). It is then stated that MHWs enhance water column
stability (no evidence provided), alleviate light limitation (no evidence provided), and
accelerate ice melt (no evidence provided), the latter alleviating iron stress (but
wouldn’t this only be immediately adjacent to melting ice?). So apparently the
suggestion in ‘a’ above about increased light alleviating iron stress was not based on
the presumption of changes in cellular stoichiometries for Fe.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for these insightful points. In the revised manuscript, we
have restructured this section to present a more nuanced, evidence-based discussion of
co-limitation and physical drivers in the Antarctic Zone. Specifically:
(1) Seasonal variability of limitation regimes
We agree that light limitation is more pronounced in winter and early spring, while co-
limitation by light and iron typically emerges during the growing season. We have
clarified that our analysis focuses on biologically active periods—when MHWs
intersect with phytoplankton growth potential (i.e., austral spring to autumn)—and not
on the full annual cycle. We now explicitly note that light limitation dominates in winter
and that MHWs occurring during non-productive months are unlikely to yield
significant biological responses.
(2) Mechanisms supporting enhanced phytoplankton growth during MHWs
 Water column stability: We now reference Hayashida et al. (2020) and Sun et al.
(2024), who show that MHWs are often accompanied by stronger stratification and
reduced mixed layer depth, particularly in the Antarctic Zone.
 Alleviation of light limitation: We cite Doney et al. (2006), who reported that
shallower mixed layers associated with warming events increased mean irradiance
exposure for phytoplankton in the euphotic zone.
 Sea ice melt and iron supply: We have revised this explanation to emphasize that
relief from iron limitation due to MHW-induced sea ice melt is strongest near the
ice edge (Richaud et al., 2024). However, we also note that iron-rich meltwater can
be advected over mesoscale distances and influence productivity in broader regions,
as supported by Loscher et al. (1997), De Baar et al. (2001), and Lannuzel et al.
(2007).
(3) Clarification of mechanism
We confirm that our explanation does not rely on changes in cellular Fe stoichiometry.
Rather, we describe how MHW-driven environmental changes may simultaneously
mitigate light and iron constraints—through physical processes—thereby facilitating a
more favorable environment for phytoplankton growth in regions that are typically co-
limited.
c. (line 197-199) Here it is stated that enhanced mixing in the STZ (no evidence
provided) alleviates nitrate limitation and promotes phytoplankton growth. First, the
assumption here is that the increase in chlorophyll in the STZ during MCS is due to an
increase in biomass. IF the supposition is correct that the mixed layer deepens during
an MCS, how do the authors know that the change in chlorophyll isn’t simply
photoacclimation to lower average mixed layer light levels? If it is an increase in
nutrient supply, one would have to show that the increase in mixing depth was sufficient
to penetrate the nutricline, otherwise there is no strong reason to think that the deeper
mixing (how much deeper, by the way, a few meters, tens of meters?) impacted nutrient
supply. Second, it is then stated that the deeper mixing during MCS in the SAZ and AZ
caused greater light limitation. But it was stated prior to this that these regions are also
iron limited (actually, during summer months they are iron limited more than light
limited, as in situ iron fertilization experiments have shown). No explanation is
provided why deeper mixing in the SAZ and AZ doesn’t also increase iron supply to
the mixed layer. Finally, be careful with the word ‘growth’. Do you mean cell division
rates or changes in biomass. The two are not the same. The mechanisms you discuss
are relevant to division rate, but what you observed from space are changes in biomass,
which are also controlled by loss processes (which are barely mentioned at all in this
manuscript).
Reply: We appreciate this detailed and insightful comment. In the revised manuscript,
we have significantly restructured this section to address these key concerns. Below we
summarize the main clarifications and revisions made:
(1) Biomass vs. Photoacclimation
We agree that observed increases in surface Chl-a could reflect changes in biomass,
cellular pigmentation, or both. To address this:
(a) We now include an analysis of satellite-derived particulate backscatter (bbp(443))
to estimate phytoplankton carbon, which supports biomass increases during MCSs (see
Extended Data Fig. 4).
(b) We explicitly note that changes in the Chl-a:carbon ratio (θ) indicate contributions
from both biomass and photoacclimation.
(c) The revised text avoids assuming a direct translation from Chl-a to biomass and
acknowledges physiological responses as a possible factor.
(2) MLD Deepening and Nutricline Penetration
We now cite GLORYS12V1 reanalysis data showing that during MCSs, the MLD
increased by an average of 4.25 ± 0.92 m globally, and by 20–30 m in the Atlantic and
Pacific sectors of the STZ. These regions are adjacent to the Southern Ocean’s winter
deep mixing band, where nutrient-rich waters are entrained into the euphotic zone. We
added supporting references (e.g., Rigby et al., 2020) to show that nutrient supply
increases are plausible in these regions during MCSs.
(3) Iron Supply in SAZ and AZ:
We have clarified that while deeper mixing during MCSs may supply some iron, the
effect is limited. In the AZ, deeper mixing also leads to reduced light availability and
enhanced sea ice formation, which scavenges dissolved iron (e.g., Lannuzel et al., 2007),
resulting in net iron removal. In the SAZ, while nitrate is abundant, iron remains the
primary limiting factor, and the modest deepening during MCSs is unlikely to deliver
sufficient iron from subsurface reservoirs.
(4) Division Rate vs. Biomass Accumulation
We thank the reviewer for this important distinction. The revised text now clearly
separates division rates (influenced by nutrient and light availability) and net biomass
change (the satellite-observed signal, governed by the balance between growth and loss
processes (e.g., grazing, sinking)). We now state that “the observed biomass anomalies
reflect net outcomes of phytoplankton division and loss rates,” aligning with the
framework proposed by Behrenfeld (2014) and others.
d. (lines 200-201) This is a repeat of the sentence before.
Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. We have removed this part in the revised
manuscript.
e.(line 202) ‘Massive’? I don’t see any evidence of ‘massive’ responses. In the STZ,
chlorophyll in places increased by 20% or so, but 20% greater than what? I’m guessing
the baseline concentrations are pretty low (e.g., see figure 4), so a 20% increase above
a low value is still a small increase.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We agree that the term “massive”
was not quantitatively justified given the relatively modest absolute changes in
chlorophyll-a concentrations, particularly in oligotrophic regions such as the STZ. We
have removed this term in the revised manuscript to ensure the language more
accurately reflects the observed magnitudes.
f. (lines 203–204) Iron is a nutrient too, so the fact that nitrate is always replete says
nothing about how phytoplankton will respond to increased nutrient supply.
Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. We have removed this part in the revised
manuscript.
g. (lines 205-206) Here the authors invoke temperature limitation. How does this play
into iron and light limitation. What is the absolute magnitude of changes in SST during
MHWs and MCSs? From figure 3, it looks like we are talking about small (generally
<2 ºC) changes. What evidence is there that these small SST changes would have a
significant impact on division rates?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that SST
anomalies during MHWs and MCSs in the Southern Ocean are typically modest—
generally <2 °C, as shown in Figure 3—and that such small changes may not directly
constrain or enhance phytoplankton division rates in isolation. As noted in previous
studies (e.g., Arrigo et al., 2012; Vehmaa & Salonen, 2009), phytoplankton blooms can
occur even in near-freezing waters, and low temperatures do not necessarily inhibit
biomass accumulation. Furthermore, temperature changes of this magnitude are often
less influential than concurrent shifts in iron availability, light exposure, and grazing
pressure. For example, reduced temperatures during MCSs may indirectly favor net
biomass accumulation by lowering zooplankton grazing rates (López-Urrutia, 2008;
Taucher & Oschlies, 2011), while deeper mixing may enhance nutrient supply
irrespective of thermal effects. In light of this, we have removed the reference to
temperature limitation as a primary control and revised the discussion to focus on the
interaction of temperature with physical and ecological processes, rather than invoking
direct thermal limitation of growth. We appreciate the reviewer’s comment, which
helped us clarify and strengthen this part of the manuscript.
h. (lines 207-209) Here it is stated that MCSs in the AZ promote sea ice formation and
this absorbs dissolved iron. What evidence do you have that sea ice formation changed
significantly during the MCSs? If it did increase, these areas of sea ice formation would
not provide valid satellite chlorophyll retrievals would they? I’m also not aware of ice
formation drawing iron out of surrounding waters, only trapping the iron in the water
that is being frozen, so I don’t see how sea ice formation would significantly impact
iron levels away from the sea ice (i.e., in the waters where you get satellite chlorophyll
data).
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. We agree that the link
between sea ice formation and iron dynamics is nuanced and that direct observational
evidence of MCS-induced changes in iron availability is limited—particularly in
satellite-accessible, ice-free regions. Our original statement aimed to present a
hypothesized mechanism rather than a confirmed effect. In the revised manuscript, we
now clarify the following:
(1) Sea ice formation and iron sequestration
During ice formation, dissolved iron can become trapped within the forming sea ice
matrix (De Baar et al., 2001; Lannuzel et al., 2007). This process reduces the
availability of iron in the surrounding water column, but primarily within the immediate
zone of ice formation.
(2) Limitations of satellite observations

Response to Reviewer #3
(Note: Reviewer comments in black and our point-to-point replies in blue)
Key Results
The authors investigate the response of phytoplankton size structures in the Southern
Ocean during marine heat waves (MHW) and marine cold spells (MCS) using a suite
of satellite-based data and modelling approaches. Their results showed MHWs were
most frequent in the Subtropics and Subantarctic. Contrasting this, they found that
MCSs were more frequent in the Antarctic Zone. Some of the results section on the
response of phytoplankton (and their size classes) to MHWs and MCSs were difficult
to follow - I have highlighted some examples below in the section on clarity. The
authors show that during MCSs in the Subtropical Zone, picoplankton increased
whereas in the Antarctic and Subantarctic Zone micro and nano plankton decreased.
They also show that the inverse was true for MHW, with micro and nano size classes
increasing in the Antarctic Zone. I think that it is an excellent idea to study the effects
of MHWs and MCSs on phytoplankton in the Southern Ocean. However, the methods
and data used in this study are not reproducible, and the choice of data products is not
detailed, and in some cases poorly chosen. As such I cannot recommend this article for
publication and suggest that this article is not accepted. Below, I have detailed my
reasoning, and I hope that the authors find my feedback helpful and constructive. If the
authors choose to resumbit the paper, I strongly suggest that they vigorously consider
and scrutinise their choice of data and methods.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback.
We fully acknowledge the concerns raised regarding methodological clarity, data
product selection, and result interpretation. In response, we have undertaken a
comprehensive revision of the manuscript. Major changes include:
(1) Substantial restructuring of the Results section to improve clarity and flow.
(2) Replacement of previously used data products with those more appropriate for
Southern Ocean conditions, such as regionally validated chlorophyll-a algorithms and
PSC-based phytoplankton size estimation.
(3) Removal of less robust analyses (e.g., the CSD slope model) and addition of
validation using in situ data where available.
(4) Clearer description of methods and data sources to ensure reproducibility, now
detailed in both the main text and Supplementary Information.
We have also refined the Discussion to ensure that interpretations are well-supported
and more cautiously framed. Figures have been updated accordingly to reflect these
improvements. We hope these substantial revisions address the reviewer’s concerns and
improve the scientific rigor and clarity of the manuscript.
Validity
Based on the figures provided, I believe that the interpretations of these results support
the trends of phytoplankton size classes during MHW and MCS events. However, I
think that their discussion on the biogeochemical / environment drivers underpinning
these changes requires further work. There is no mention of phytoplankton groups or
taxonomy. For example, in the Subantarctic Zone haptophytes (E. hux) dominate (Balch et al., 2014). It is widely recognised that in the Antarctic Zone diatoms and haptophyes (P. antarctica) are dominant (Smith et al., 2014; Hayward et al., 2024). These different groups, and species within them, respond differently to environmental stimuli. As such, the discussion on phytoplankton size classes should be accompanied by discussing phytoplankton speciation and phenology.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that taxonomic
composition plays a key role in shaping regional phytoplankton responses and that
species-level differences are critical for interpreting size-based trends. In the revised
Discussion, we have included additional context referencing the dominant taxa in each
zone—such as Emiliania huxleyi in the Subantarctic Zone and diatoms and Phaeocystis
antarctica in the Antarctic Zone (Balch et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2014; Hayward et al.,
2024)—and have noted how their differing ecophysiological traits may contribute to
the observed patterns in size structure during MHW and MCS events. We also clarify
the limitations of our approach: the PSC algorithm used in this study estimates size
class composition but cannot resolve species or functional group taxonomy. We now
explicitly acknowledge this constraint and highlight that integrating satellite data with
in situ taxonomic observations and functional trait modeling represents an important
avenue for future work.
Significance
I think that these results would be significant and important to biogeochemists,
ecosystem modellers and earth system scientists. However, I struggle to move past the
poorly detailed methods and data used in the study.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the broader relevance of our
findings and acknowledge the concern regarding insufficient methodological detail. In
response, we have thoroughly revised the Methods section to improve transparency and
reproducibility. Key updates include:
(1) Explicit identification and justification of all data products used;
(2) Clear definitions of MHW and MCS criteria;
(3) Detailed descriptions of anomaly calculations, temporal smoothing, and spatial
gridding;
(4) An expanded explanation of the PSC-based size class estimation and associated
validation steps.
Data and methodology
The methods and data used in this manuscript lack scientific rigour and are not
reproducible. This is primarily the reason I am not accepting this article. I have detailed
my reasoning thoroughly below. The data used in the study would benefit from clearer
definition and more detailed justification to ensure it is well-suited to the study's
objectives. For chlorophyll a (Chl-a) data the authors state that they used ‘chlorophyll
from CMEMS’. A CMEMS database search showed there are 54 different Chl-a
products available on CMEMS. See Pauthenet et al., (2024) which details differences
in commonly used Chl-a products. It is very important to specify what product is used
to ensure results are reproducible, but to also further understand potential uncertainties
and biases. The authors should state what CMEMS product was chosen and why it was
used in the study. Furthermore, it has not been possible to assess any code as in the
‘code availability’ statement, all the authors said was that the analysis was conducted
in Matlab.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for highlighting these important issues. In the revised
manuscript, we have taken the following steps to address your concerns:
(1) Chlorophyll-a Product Specification and Justification
We have removed the ambiguous reference to "chlorophyll from CMEMS" and now
clearly state in the Methods section that we use daily R data from the ESA Ocean
rs
Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI v6.0, https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00281).
This product was selected for its long-term consistency and its improved performance
in the Southern Ocean when paired with region-specific algorithms (e.g., Johnson et al.,
2013; Pauthenet et al., 2024). We applied the OC4v6 algorithm, adapted for the
Southern Ocean, to estimate surface chlorophyll-a concentrations. The rationale for this
choice and its advantages over other products are now clearly explained.
(2) Improved Reproducibility and Code Availability:
We recognize the importance of code transparency for reproducibility. In the revised
Code Availability section, we now state that all scripts used in this study, written in
MATLAB, are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
Additionally, key code components for processing chlorophyll-a, computing
MHWs/MCSs, and performing anomaly analysis have been documented and included
in the Supplementary Information as pseudocode to enhance transparency.
The authors use surface reflectances from MODIS-Aqua for their size class model. The
time series for MODIS-Aqua (May - 2002 to 2024) is shorter than their study period
(1998 - 2022). Furthermore, in 2019 MODIS-Aqua drifted out of orbit. There is
a disclaimer on the NASA website suggesting that data from ~2019 should be treated
with caution. As such, I would not trust the PSC / CDS results from 2019 - 2022 in this
study from MODIS-Aqua.
Reply: Thank you for raising this critical point. In the revised manuscript, we no longer
use MODIS-Aqua reflectance data. To ensure consistency across the full study period
(1998–2022) and to address concerns related to post-2019 MODIS-Aqua data quality,
we now use daily R from the ESA Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI
rs
v6.0), which provides a consistent multi-sensor merged product with rigorous inter-
sensor calibration and gap-filling. We then apply a Southern Ocean–specific
chlorophyll-a algorithm to this OC-CCI Rrs dataset, enhancing both the temporal
continuity and the accuracy of chlorophyll estimates. This change ensures that our
phytoplankton size class estimates—derived using the PSC model—are based on a
higher-quality and longer-term dataset. We have revised the Methods section to reflect
these changes and have removed all reliance on MODIS-Aqua data.
The authors use the OISSTv2 product in their study to assess MHW and MCS. This
product is one of the older products used in SST remote sensing and no longer
considered the ‘gold standard’ (instead, see the SST CCI). The product is also of coarse
spatial resolution (.25 degrees) compared to more modern products, and does not match
the spatial resolution of chlorophyll data (4km). The authors interpolated the chl-a
product to make it coarser and on the same grid as the OISST product. In doing so they
will miss out on many of the finer scale processes in the dataset. One of the largest
caveats of this study is that the remote sensing of sea surface temperatures is not
possible for much of the year in polar regions due to ice cover. Where there is sea ice
the OISST algorithm estimates the under ice SST by a linear fit capped at -1.8 celsius.
As such, the MCSs observed in this study are not the result of actual satellite
observations, but could in fact be due to how the OISST product handles under ice
temperatures.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed feedback. In the revised manuscript, we
addressed these concerns as follows:
(1) Updated SST Product:
We replaced the OISSTv2 dataset with the more advanced ESA Sea Surface
Temperature Climate Change Initiative (ESA SST CCI v3.0) reanalysis product, which
provides improved accuracy, inter-sensor consistency, and bias correction suitable for
long-term climate analyses in polar regions.
(2) Sea Ice Considerations:
To mitigate the limitations of SST retrieval under ice cover, we applied a mask to
exclude regions with an annual average sea ice concentration (SIC) greater than 20%.
This reduces the likelihood of including SST anomalies that are artifacts of the under-
ice estimation algorithm used in SST datasets (as noted by the reviewer).
(3) Spatial Resolution Harmonization:
While we acknowledge that regridding the high-resolution chlorophyll-a product (OC-
CCI, native 4 km) to 0.25° resolution may reduce sensitivity to submesoscale variability,
we opted for this approach to maintain consistency across all parameters analyzed
(including SST, nutrients, and MLD). This facilitates robust spatial alignment in the
detection and attribution of MHW/MCS events and their ecological impacts. We have
now explicitly stated this limitation in the revised Methods and Discussion sections.
These updates ensure higher data fidelity and improve the robustness of our conclusions
regarding phytoplankton responses to thermal extremes in the Southern Ocean.
The methods section is very short, and there is no information provided on the CSD
model, other than a short description in the supplementary information. The PSC model
used was recently published (2023); and the PSC model is dependent on SST
observations. There should be discussion regarding uncertainty model uncertainty and
performance, especially when there can be issues of circularity as both the size class
model use SST and the authors investigate the response of size classes to MHWs and
MCSs.
Reply: Thank you for this important comment. In the revised manuscript, we have fully
removed the CSD model and associated analyses to improve methodological clarity and
focus. Regarding the PSC model (Sun et al., 2023), we acknowledge that it uses SST
as one of its key input variables. To address concerns about potential circularity—where
SST is used both to define MHW/MCS events and as a driver of phytoplankton size
class estimates—we took the following steps:
(1) Independent Validation:
We validated the PSC-derived phytoplankton size class outputs against in situ
observations from the Southern Ocean (1998–2023), which demonstrated good
agreement (details provided in the revised Methods and Supplementary Figures).
(2) Clarified Use of SST:
While SST is used in both MHW/MCS classification and as an input to the PSC model,
these serve distinct functions: (i) in the former, SST is used to define the timing and
intensity of thermal anomalies; (ii) in the latter, SST is used as an ecophysiological
proxy influencing phytoplankton size structure. We now explicitly acknowledge this
dual role in the Discussion, and we clarify that our analyses focus on relative anomalies
in size structure during MHWs and MCSs, rather than directly correlating SST with
size class output.
(3) Model Justification:
Previous studies (e.g., Sun et al., 2023; Moore et al., 2020) have shown that
phytoplankton size composition may vary substantially under environmental stress
even when total chlorophyll-a remains unchanged. SST has proven effective in
detecting these shifts in ecological niches. Thus, the PSC model remains a valuable tool
for interpreting community-scale responses to thermal extremes.
These clarifications and validations are now fully incorporated into the revised Methods
and Discussion sections.
Finally, there is inconsistency in the date ranges. Chl-a observations are only available
during summer high latitudes, and many observations are not possible due to satellites
not being able to assess ocean colour during periods of ice cover. Furthermore, the
baseline and time series of Chl-a will be shorter than the baseline of the SST product,
adding further inconsistencies.
Reply: Thank you for this insightful comment. We acknowledge that satellite-derived
chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) observations in high-latitude regions are seasonally limited,
primarily due to ice cover and reduced daylight during winter months. To minimize the
influence of inconsistent data coverage, we implemented the following measures in the
revised manuscript:
(1) Sea Ice Masking:
We applied a conservative mask to exclude regions with an annual average sea ice
concentration greater than 20%, thereby focusing our analysis on open-water areas
where satellite Chl-a retrievals are consistently valid.
(2) Aligned Time Windows:
While the SST dataset spans 1982–2023, the Chl-a dataset covers 1998–2023. To ensure
consistency, all analyses involving phytoplankton responses to MHWs and MCSs were
restricted to events occurring between 1998 and 2023—the common period for both
SST and Chl-a datasets.
(3) Climatology Construction:
Daily climatologies for both SST and Chl-a were constructed independently using their
respective time windows. Although their baseline periods differ (SST: 1982–2011; Chl-
a: 1998–2023), all anomaly analyses were constrained within the Chl-a observation
period, ensuring internal consistency in the biological response evaluations.
These steps ensure that our comparisons are methodologically sound and that observed
phytoplankton responses are not biased by inconsistent temporal coverage. This
clarification has been included in the revised Methods and Discussion sections.
Clarity and Context
Overall, the clarity of the manuscript could be tightened and improved. There are lots
of ‘they’ and ‘this’ without explicitly specifying what is changing and why. Furthermore,
the structure could be improved by using more subheadings. For example:
‘Phytoplankton Size classes during a MHW,’ and ‘Phytoplankton size classes during a
MCS’. The authors can then address each size class separately in different paragraphs
to improve the readability.
Reply: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have
substantially improved clarity by eliminating vague pronouns and clearly specifying
subjects and changes throughout the text. We have also restructured the Results and
Discussion sections to improve readability by introducing descriptive subheadings,
such as “Phytoplankton size classes during MHWs” and “Phytoplankton size classes
during MCSs.” Furthermore, responses of each size class are now addressed in
dedicated paragraphs, making the narrative more organized and accessible for readers.
On line 144:
Microplankton demonstrated apparent variability at the polar front; north of the polar front, they maintained a negative
response; however, south of the polar front, their response shifted to a positive phase, indicating significant proliferation in
the Antarctic zone.
Dissecting this passage, it is difficult to understand what ‘apparent variability’ means, increasing, decreasing? Following
this, the authors say that it ‘maintained a negative’ response. What are they responding to, a MHW a MCS, this isn’t clear at
all.
Reply: Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that the original sentence was
ambiguous and lacked clarity regarding the direction and cause of the response. In the
revised manuscript, we have removed this sentence and rephrased the surrounding text
to more explicitly describe the response of microplankton to MHWs and MCSs with
respect to both location (north vs. south of the polar front) and event type. This revision
ensures that both the direction of change and the environmental driver are clearly stated.
In the opening line to a paragraph on line 117: ‘The temporal evolution of these responses further highlighted their
complexity (Fig. 4)’. The authors need to be clear as to what ‘these responses’ are, especially if they are opening a
paragraph with this statement; similarly, the authors should define what ‘their complexities’ are. Don’t leave it to the reader to
try and guess what you are trying to convey. In academic writing, for any journal, try to really spell these things out, be clear
and avoid vague language.
Reply: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback. We agree that the
original phrasing was too vague. In the revised manuscript, we have clarified that “these
responses” refer specifically to the temporal variations in the fractional contributions
of micro-, nano-, and picoplankton during marine heatwaves (MHWs) and marine cold
spells (MCSs). We also expanded the sentence to explain that “their complexity” refers
to the non-uniform, regionally dependent, and often nonlinear temporal patterns
observed across different phytoplankton size classes and oceanographic zones. This
revision enhances the clarity and scientific precision of the paragraph's opening and sets
a clearer context for the discussion that follows.
The abstract states (line 8): MHWs suppressed phytoplankton growth in the subtropical zone but stimulated it in the sub-
Antarctic and Antarctic zones by alleviating light and iron limitations.
There is nowhere in the study that iron or light is investigated. I do not understand how the authors can state this in their
abstract.
Reply: Thank you for your careful reading and insightful comment. We fully agree that
the original sentence in the abstract overstated the scope of our analysis, as the
manuscript does not directly quantify iron or light availability. To maintain scientific
rigor and avoid unsupported interpretations, we have removed this sentence from the
abstract in the revised manuscript. Instead, we now focus on the observed
phytoplankton responses to MHWs and MCSs, without attributing causality to specific
environmental drivers that were not explicitly analyzed. We appreciate your feedback,
which helped us improve the accuracy and focus of our abstract.
References
The manuscript is oddly referenced. For example, reference 9 is in relation to Southern Ocean MHWs, but the citation
describes MHWs in the South Atlantic. Reference 13 is provided in the context of MCSs in the Southern Ocean, however the
reference is located in the North Sea.
Reply: Thank you for pointing this out. We have carefully reviewed all references in
the revised manuscript to ensure they are contextually accurate and regionally
appropriate. Specifically, references 9 and 13 have been replaced with peer-reviewed
studies that directly investigate marine heatwaves and cold spells in the Southern Ocean.
We also conducted a broader check of all citations to verify that each one accurately
supports the corresponding statement. We appreciate your attention to detail, which has
helped improve the scholarly integrity of our manuscript.
References
Balch WM, Bates NR, Lam PJ, Twining BS, Rosengard SZ, Bowler BC, et al. Factors
regulating the Great Calcite Belt in the Southern Ocean and its biogeochemical significance.
Global Biogeochemical Cycles 2016, 30(8), 1124-1144.
Smith Jr WO, Ainley DG, Arrigo KR, Dinniman, MS. The oceanography and ecology of the
Ross Sea. Annual review of marine science 2014, 6(1), 469-487.
Hayward A, Pinkerton MH, Wright SW, Gutiérrez-Rodriguez A, Law CS. Twenty-six years of
phytoplankton pigments reveal a circumpolar Class Divide around the Southern Ocean.
Communications Earth & Environment 2024, 5(1), 92.
Pauthenet E, Martinez E, Gorgues T, Roussillon J, Drumetz L, Fablet R, Roux M. Contrasted
trends in chlorophyll‐a satellite products. Geophysical Research Letters 2024, 51(14),
e2024GL108916.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: I believe that the authors have adequately addressed the issues raised in my first review.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript analyses phytoplankton chlorophyll-a, carbon, and phytoplankton size classes (PSC) responses to marine
heatwaves (MHWs) and marine cold spells (MCSs) across Southern Ocean water masses, using satellite observations,
model reanalysis, and autonomous Argo profiles. The topic is timely, and the multi-platform approach is a real strength. I
appreciate the scope of the work and the effort to link physical extremes with biological responses across latitudinal
gradients and water masses in the Southern Ocean.
At times, I found the narrative hard to follow, and I think clarity could be strengthened. The study is clearly about
phytoplankton responses to temperature extremes, but the central take-home message is not consistently articulated across
sections. Parts of the Results section were difficult to follow. For example, at line 119 it is unclear whether the reported
51.7% refers to positive or negative anomalies. In the Conclusions, the statement that “Chl-a concentrations exhibit
symmetrical responses during extreme high and low temperatures” would benefit from a precise reference frame:
symmetrical relative to what: temperature anomaly magnitude, chlorophyll anomaly magnitude, or another metric? A similar
issue arises at line 134, where “The temporal evolution of these responses further highlighted their complexity” begins a
paragraph without specifying what “these” are and what kind of “complexity” is meant, which makes the thread difficult to
follow. Consider explicitly framing results with subheadings by latitude bands / water masses and closing each subsection
with a one-sentence takeaway; this could substantially improve readability. Similarly, frame what the paragraph is about in
the first line.
Stronger framing and definitions at the start of the Results could also help. A concise description of the datasets and explicit
definitions of MHWs/CSs, including the time and anomaly thresholds you adopt, would orient readers. It would also help to
define what constitutes an “event” in your workflow. Under a pixel-level Hobday-style detection, a value such as 0.14 events
per decade is ambiguous (e.g., is an event tied to a single pixel? Under Hobday’s definition it can be). Many studies use %
or area covered, which could aid interpretation here. Reporting area affected by MHWs/MCSs alongside event counts
(number of pixels) would make the results more interpretable. If you use the Hobday et al. (2018) severity categories,
introducing these before they first appear would help readers who are familiar with phytoplankton ecology, but not MHWs.
Regional terminology and masking needs to be clarified. The zone referred to as the “Antarctic Zone” appears, from the
figures, to correspond more closely to the Permanently Open Ocean Zone (POOOZ/POOZ; see Deppeler & Davidson,
2017), with much of the true Antarctic Zone masked. This distinction matters for interpretation; without the figures, one would
assume the Antarctic Zone to be closer to Antarctica. In sea-ice regions, satellites do not retrieve SST beneath ice and a
practical baseline near −1.8 °C is often implied; this will influence MHW/MCS identification, severity classification, and any
zonal comparisons, so it would be helpful to state that these areas are masked. This also raises a question about the
analysis period: is it year-round, or focused on summer? The seasonal signal could be strong, so a seasonal breakdown
might provide useful context. Similarly, summer in Antarctica is more free of ice and can allow clearer MHW/Chl-a trend
detection, filling in this data gap in your study, see examples in Pinkerton et al., (2021), or Hayward et al., (2025).
Several statements would benefit from supporting evidence or softer phrasing. At line 256, “Mixed layer reduced loss rates
through greater population dilution and decreased grazing pressure” reads as a process explanation but has no direct
support from observations, modelling, or citations. If this reflects the authors’ interpretation, it needs to be framed as a
hypothesis with references.
Given the diversity of the datasets, uncertainty metrics would be very helpful. Pigment-to-PSC relationships usually show
good agreement, but are complicated by pigment sharing among taxa, which affects diagnostic partitioning. The manuscript
mentions a 17-variable PSC model, but the rationale for this choice, and the validation from HPLC pigments to size classes
are not described. In the validation, the HPLC data alone do not inherently yield size classes; there are multiple diagnostic
pigment approaches, so additional methodological detail needs to be stated. As the key conclusions rely on PSC outputs,
more information on methods and uncertainty would greatly improve the paper. If SST is used as an input to the PSC model,
a brief discussion of potential circularity when analysing responses to temperature extremes, and how this was mitigated,
e.g. via sensitivity testing, potentially without SST would provide more confidence in the results.
It would also be useful to briefly discuss the choice of MHW definition. MHW definitions greatly influence identification and
severity, and there is ongoing debate about methodological sensitivity. If you adopt the Hobday et al. framework, detail why
it suits this study, see Farchadi et al. (2025, Nature Climate Change, “Marine heatwaves are in the eye of the beholder”).
A few line-specific clarifications could further improve the manuscript. At line 26, please specify the regions where previously
identified impacts of MHWs occurred. Between lines 47 and 50, the juxtaposition of a “decline in chlorophyll-a” with
“extensive algal blooms” reads as contradictory and needs rephrasing.
The citations need another check. Despite stating they had been fixed, some references appear to be irrelevant to the paper.
Review 10 is presented as Southern Ocean but is about the Atlantic, and citation 13 addresses North Sea sole and does not
fit the scope at all. Similarly, a few highly relevant studies on latitudinal patterns in chlorophyll-a and phytoplankton
composition have been missed, including Schlosser et al. (2025), “Latitudinal trends in drivers of the Southern Ocean spring
bloom onset” (JGR); Hayward et al. (2024), “Twenty-six years of phytoplankton pigments reveal a circumpolar class divide
around the Southern Ocean” (Communications Earth & Environment); and Pinkerton et al. (2021), “Evidence for the Impact
of Climate Change on Primary Producers in the Southern Ocean” (Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution).
In summary, the manuscript addresses an important problem and uses multi-platform datasets. However, there are several
components of the study that needs addressing before publication. First, the narrative and framing needs to be improved,
with the conclusions and take home messages clearly stated. I think that the methods needs to be far more detailed to be
easily replicated by others. Most importantly, some level of uncertainty needs to be quantified as so much data from so many
sources are used.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:

I believe that the authors have adequately addressed the issues raised in my first review.

(Note: Reviewer comments in black and our point-to-point replies in blue)

classes (PSC) responses to marine heatwaves (MHWs) and marine cold spells (MCSs)

our multi-platform approach. Following your constructive suggestions, we have
carefully revised the manuscript, substantially improving the clarity, precision, and
overall quality of the paper.

The study is clearly about phytoplankton responses to temperature extremes, but the

Reply: We sincerely thank you for your valuable suggestions. We have followed your
guidance to enhance the clarity of the manuscript and ensure that the responses of
phytoplankton to extreme temperature events are consistently communicated
throughout. Our specific revisions are as follows:
(1) Regarding unclear percentages such as 51.7%, we carefully reviewed the
descriptions throughout the manuscript and supplemented all instances where the sign
of the anomaly percentages were not explicitly specified (please refer to line 124).
(2) The statement that Chl-a concentrations exhibit corresponding responses during
extreme high and low temperatures lacked a clear reference frame. We have now
clarified that the phytoplankton responses are symmetrical relative to the Chl-a anomaly
magnitude (Please refer to line 308).
(3) The original sentence “The temporal evolution of these responses further
highlighted their complexity” was unclear. We revised it to: “The temporal evolution
of phytoplankton Chl-a anomalies during MHWs and MCSs reveals distinct patterns
across regions” (Please refer to line 141).
(4) We emphasized the focus of each paragraph at its beginning and added concise
summaries at the end of each subsection to more clearly convey the main points and
improve the readability of the manuscript.
Stronger framing and definitions at the start of the Results could also help. A concise
description of the datasets and explicit definitions of MHWs/CSs, including the time
and anomaly thresholds you adopt, would orient readers. It would also help to define
what constitutes an “event” in your workflow. Under a pixel-level Hobday-style
detection, a value such as 0.14 events per decade is ambiguous (e.g., is an event tied to
a single pixel? Under Hobday’s definition it can be). Many studies use % or area
covered, which could aid interpretation here. Reporting area affected by MHWs/MCSs
alongside event counts (number of pixels) would make the results more interpretable.
If you use the Hobday et al. (2018) severity categories, introducing these before they
first appear would help readers who are familiar with phytoplankton ecology, but not
MHWs.
Reply: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have now added an introduction
to the datasets and provided explicit definitions of MHWs and MCSs at the beginning
of the Results section, including the baseline period and thresholds used, to improve
readability and clarity of the manuscript. In our workflow, an “event” represents the
occurrence of a single MHW or MCS at a given grid cell. However, the original use of
“event” in the text was not precise. To better convey our meaning, we have replaced
“event” with “times” to indicate the number of MHW or MCS occurrences, which is
more accurate. Furthermore, before presenting results of the severity classification,
we introduced the Hobday-style classification framework. This allows a more reasonable
assessment of phytoplankton responses under extreme temperature events of different
intensities. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this suggestion, which has improved
the clarity and logical flow of our manuscript.
Regional terminology and masking needs to be clarified. The zone referred to as the
“Antarctic Zone” appears, from the figures, to correspond more closely to the
Permanently Open Ocean Zone (POOOZ/POOZ; see Deppeler & Davidson, 2017),
with much of the true Antarctic Zone masked. This distinction matters for interpretation;
without the figures, one would assume the Antarctic Zone to be closer to Antarctica. In
sea-ice regions, satellites do not retrieve SST beneath ice and a practical baseline near
−1.8 °C is often implied; this will influence MHW/MCS identification, severity
classification, and any zonal comparisons, so it would be helpful to state that these areas
are masked. This also raises a question about the analysis period: is it year-round, or
focused on summer? The seasonal signal could be strong, so a seasonal breakdown
might provide useful context. Similarly, summer in Antarctica is more free of ice and
can allow clearer MHW/Chl-a trend detection, filling in this data gap in your study,
see examples in Pinkerton et al., (2021), or Hayward et al., (2025).
Reply: We thank you for these helpful suggestions, our revisions are as follows:
(1) Clarification of Antarctic Zone and masking
We agree that much of the Antarctic Zone is masked. To distinguish the permanently
open ocean area, we clarified in the Methods section that, in this study, the Antarctic
Zone is defined as the region between the Polar Front and the 20% climatological SIC
contour. To ensure accurate identification of MHWs and MCSs, severity classification,
and inter-zone comparisons, all SST data in areas with mean annual SIC greater than
20% were masked.
(2) Seasonal context and Chl-a responses
Our analysis covers the entire year, which may weaken seasonal signals. To address
this, we added descriptions of the characteristics of MHWs and MCSs across different
seasons and the responses of Chl-a during extreme temperature events. Summer in the
Southern Ocean, with minimal sea-ice coverage, allows clearer detection of extreme
temperature events and Chl-a trends. Indeed, Chl-a anomalies during MHWs are most
pronounced in summer (see Supplementary Fig. 8), effectively supplementing the
contextual information for our study.
Supplementary Fig. 8 | Spatial distribution of seasonal mean intensity of MHWs (a-d)
and MCSs (e-h) during 1998–2023, and the corresponding mean Chl-a anomaly
percentages during MHWs (i-l) and MCSs (m-p) for each season.
Several statements would benefit from supporting evidence or softer phrasing. At line
256, “Mixed layer reduced loss rates through greater population dilution and decreased
grazing pressure” reads as a process explanation but has no direct support from
observations, modelling, or citations. If this reflects the authors’ interpretation, it needs
to be framed as a hypothesis with references.
Reply: We thank you for this comment. We agree that our original phrasing implied a
mechanistic explanation without providing direct observational or modeling support.
To address this, we have revised the sentence to adopt a more cautious and hypothesis-
based framing, and we have added appropriate references. The revised sentence now
reads:“The increased nutrient supply may have elevated phytoplankton division rates,
especially for fast-growing diatoms, while the deeper mixed layer may have contributed
to reduced loss rates, potentially through greater population dilution and decreased
grazing pressure (Behrenfeld & Boss, 2018; Diaz et al., 2021).” We believe this
modification softens the language, makes clear that this is an interpretation rather than
a demonstrated causal mechanism, and provides references to prior studies that discuss
these processes.
Given the diversity of the datasets, uncertainty metrics would be very helpful. Pigment-
to-PSC relationships usually show good agreement, but are complicated by pigment
sharing among taxa, which affects diagnostic partitioning. The manuscript mentions a
17-variable PSC model, but the rationale for this choice, and the validation from HPLC
pigments to size classes are not described. In the validation, the HPLC data alone do
not inherently yield size classes; there are multiple diagnostic pigment approaches, so
additional methodological detail needs to be stated. As the key conclusions rely on PSC
outputs, more information on methods and uncertainty would greatly improve the paper.
If SST is used as an input to the PSC model, a brief discussion of potential circularity
when analysing responses to temperature extremes, and how this was mitigated,
e.g. via sensitivity testing, potentially without SST would provide more confidence in the
results.
Reply: Thank you very much for these valuable suggestions. We have now
supplemented our manuscript with evaluations of uncertainty metrics and sensitivity
analyses. Our specific revisions and responses are as follows:
(1) Pigments are shared among different phytoplankton groups, which affects the
classification of size structure, especially between picoplankton and nanoplankton.
HPLC data alone cannot directly produce size classes, so we processed the pigment
data according to Brewin et al. (2015), using seven diagnostic pigments to calculate the
community proportion of the three phytoplankton size classes. This approach accounts
for the fact certain pigments (e.g. 19′-hexanoyloxyfucoxanthin and fucoxanthin) are
found among phytoplankton in different size classes. The technique has also been
independently evaluated against measurements of Chl-a in the three size classes derived
from sequential-based, size-fractionated filtration (see Figure 2 of Brewin et al. 2017,
https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2017.00104). The specific formulas are provided in the
Methods (please refer to lines 462-489). Additionally, we have uploaded the calculation
code used in this study to facilitate rapid reproducibility of our results.
(2) We apologize for the previous misstatement. We employed a 17-parameter PSC
model rather than a 17-variable model. The coefficients of the PSC model are functions
of SST (Supplementary Text 1). The model only requires Chl-a and SST as input
variables, but the model itself has inherent uncertainty. The model developers (Sun et
al., 2023) provided the 5.55% and 94.45% confidence intervals (equivalent to ±2
standard deviations) for the 17 parameters. We performed 3,000 Monte Carlo
simulations within this range to calculate the confidence interval bandwidth and
standard deviation of the PSC outputs to quantify model uncertainty and found that
overall uncertainty is relatively low (see Supplementary Fig. 10).
(3) We also thank you again for your suggestion regarding potential circularity, as SST
is both an input to the PSC model and the environmental variable of interest in our study
of extreme temperatures. To address this, we performed a sensitivity analysis by
calculating the standard deviation of the SST and Chl-a datasets and applying
perturbation coefficients ranging from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1, multiplied by the
standard deviation to create new perturbed datasets. Our results indicate that the PSC
model is most sensitive to changes in Chl-a, while SST also affects the outputs,
primarily influencing picoplankton, which are more responsive to temperature changes.
In contrast, microplankton, with larger cell sizes, are barely affected by SST
perturbations (see Supplementary Fig. 11).
Sun et al. (2023) also provided a PSC model variant without SST input, using only Chl-
a. We validated this no-SST model in the Southern Ocean against in situ datasets and
found its performance for picoplankton was relatively poor (r = 0.54; see
Supplementary Fig. 12), likely because picoplankton are more sensitive to
environmental changes, and Chl-a alone cannot fully capture their subtle variations.
Therefore, SST is necessary to improve model accuracy. Nevertheless, we additionally
validated the anomalous variations in the outputs of the PSC model without SST input
during MHWs and MCSs (see Supplementary Fig. 13). The results demonstrate that,
even without SST input, the conclusions of this study remain valid, effectively
addressing the issue of circularity.
The study by Hayward et al. (2025) has provided valuable guidance, as they used 10
environmental variables as model inputs, achieving high model stability. In comparison,
our PSC model relies on only two environmental variables, Chl-a and SST, so changes
in either variable can substantially affect the outputs. In future work, we plan to
incorporate multiple environmental variables into the PSC model to enhance its
stability, allowing it to produce more reliable outputs under future extreme temperature
events and climate change scenarios. Once again, we sincerely thank you for your
valuable suggestions, which have greatly improved our understanding of phytoplankton
modeling and its interaction with climate variability.
Supplementary Fig.10 | Results of PSC model uncertainty analysis. (a–c) Confidence
interval bandwidths calculated from 3,000 Monte Carlo simulations within the 4.55%–
94.55% confidence interval of the PSC model parameters. (d–f) Spatial distributions of
the corresponding standard deviations.
Supplementary Fig.11 | Results of PSC model sensitivity analysis. (a) Perturbations
applied to Chl-a and (b) perturbations applied to SST. The perturbation magnitude is
defined as a coefficient ranging from 0 to 1 (with an interval of 0.1) multiplied by the
standard deviation of the dataset.
Supplementary Fig.12 | Validation between in-situ chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentration
and Chl-a concentration derived from the chlorophyll algorithm (OC4V6) and the PSC
model (SST-independent), including total Chl-a concentration (a), picoplankton (b),
nanoplankton (c), and microplankton (d).
Supplementary Fig.13 | Chl-a anomalies for picoplankton, nanoplankton, and
microplankton during MHWs and MCSs in the SO from 1998 to 2023. (a-c) Chl-a
anomalies for picoplankton (a), nanoplankton (b), and microplankton (c) during MHWs.
(d-f) Corresponding Chl-a anomalies during MCSs. (g-i) Box plots of phytoplankton
community fractions in the STZ, SAZ, and AZ subregions during MHW and MCS
events, respectively. The PSC model used is the version without SST input.
It would also be useful to briefly discuss the choice of MHW definition. MHW
definitions greatly influence identification and severity, and there is ongoing debate
about methodological sensitivity. If you adopt the Hobday et al. framework, detail why
it suits this study, see Farchadi et al. (2025, Nature Climate Change, “Marine heatwaves
are in the eye of the beholder”).
Reply: We thank you for highlighting the importance of carefully considering the
definition of marine heatwaves. Indeed, MHW definitions strongly influence event
detection and severity, and there is ongoing debate about the sensitivity of different
approaches. In this study, we adopted the Hobday et al. (2016) framework because it
has become a widely accepted and standardized method in the literature, facilitating
comparability across studies and regions. Specifically, we used a 30-year baseline
without detrending, which allows extreme temperature events to reflect both short-term
anomalies and the longer-term climate trend. We recognize that this approach may not
fully capture regional characteristics or isolate recent extremes. In future work, we plan
to examine the influence of alternative baselines, different SST products, and regionally
tailored definitions of MHW/MCS to better disentangle the roles of long-term climate
change and short-term variability. We have added a discussion on the definition of
MHWs in the manuscript (Please refer to lines 319-324).
A few line-specific clarifications could further improve the manuscript. At line 26,
please specify the regions where previously identified impacts of MHWs occurred.
Between lines 47 and 50, the juxtaposition of a “decline in chlorophyll-a” with
“extensive algal blooms” reads as contradictory and needs rephrasing.
Reply: We thank you for these helpful suggestions. In response:
(1) We have clarified the geographic context by specifying that the previously identified
impacts of MHWs occurred in the Southern Ocean (Please refer to line 26).
(2) We have removed the reference to “extensive algal blooms” to avoid the potential
contradiction with the observed decline in chlorophyll-a, thereby improving clarity
(Please refer to lines 47-50).
The citations need another check. Despite stating they had been fixed, some references
appear to be irrelevant to the paper. Review 10 is presented as Southern Ocean but is
about the Atlantic, and citation 13 addresses North Sea sole and does not fit the scope
at all. Similarly, a few highly relevant studies on latitudinal patterns in chlorophyll-a
and phytoplankton composition have been missed, including Schlosser et al. (2025),
“Latitudinal trends in drivers of the Southern Ocean spring bloom onset” (JGR);
Hayward et al. (2024), “Twenty-six years of phytoplankton pigments reveal a
circumpolar class divide around the Southern Ocean” (Communications Earth &
Environment); and Pinkerton et al. (2021), “Evidence for the Impact of Climate Change
on Primary Producers in the Southern Ocean” (Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution).
Reply: We thank you for pointing out the inconsistencies in the reference list and we
apologize for the oversight. We carefully re-examined all in-text citations and the
bibliography. Specifically, Reference 10 (previously an Atlantic study) has been
replaced with a more appropriate Southern Ocean reference that supports the statement
in question, and Reference 13 (North Sea sole) has been removed because it is not
relevant to the present study. In addition, we have added the reviewer-recommended,
highly relevant studies (Schlosser et al., 2025; Hayward et al., 2024; and Pinkerton et
al., 2021) and have updated the manuscript text where these citations are most
appropriate. Finally, we conducted a thorough pass over the full reference list to correct
other mismatches and ensure all citations now accurately reflect the literature
referenced in the text. Thank you for helping us improve the manuscript’s accuracy and
relevance.
In summary, the manuscript addresses an important problem and uses multi-platform
datasets. However, there are several components of the study that needs addressing
before publication. First, the narrative and framing needs to be improved, with the

reviewer #2’s comment:
c. (line 197-199) Here it is stated that enhanced mixing in the STZ (no evidence
provided) alleviates nitrate limitation and promotes phytoplankton growth. First, the
assumption here is that the increase in chlorophyll in the STZ during MCS is due to an
increase in biomass. IF the supposition is correct that the mixed layer deepens during
an MCS, how do the authors know that the change in chlorophyll isn’t simply
photoacclimation to lower average mixed layer light levels? If it is an increase in
nutrient supply, one would have to show that the increase in mixing depth was sufficient
to penetrate the nutricline, otherwise there is no strong reason to think that the deeper
mixing (how much deeper, by the way, a few meters, tens of meters?) impacted nutrient
supply. Second, it is then stated that the deeper mixing during MCS in the SAZ and AZ
caused greater light limitation. But it was stated prior to this that these regions are also
iron limited (actually, during summer months they are iron limited more than light
limited, as in situ iron fertilization experiments have shown). No explanation is
provided why deeper mixing in the SAZ and AZ doesn’t also increase iron supply to
the mixed layer. Finally, be careful with the word ‘growth’. Do you mean cell division
rates or changes in biomass. The two are not the same. The mechanisms you discuss
are relevant to division rate, but what you observed from space are changes in biomass,
which are also controlled by loss processes (which are barely mentioned at all in this
manuscript).
Reply: We appreciate this detailed and insightful comment. In the revised manuscript,
we have significantly restructured this section to address these key concerns. Below we
summarize the main clarifications and revisions made:
(1) Biomass vs. Photoacclimation
We agree that observed increases in surface Chl-a could reflect changes in biomass,
cellular pigmentation, or both. To address this:
(a) We now include an analysis of satellite-derived particulate backscatter (bbp(443))
to estimate phytoplankton carbon, which supports biomass increases during MCSs (see
Extended Data Fig. 4).
(b) We explicitly note that changes in the Chl-a:carbon ratio (θ) indicate contributions
from both biomass and photoacclimation.
(c) The revised text avoids assuming a direct translation from Chl-a to biomass and
acknowledges physiological responses as a possible factor.
(2) MLD Deepening and Nutricline Penetration
We now cite GLORYS12V1 reanalysis data showing that during MCSs, the MLD
increased by an average of 4.25 ± 0.92 m globally, and by 20–30 m in the Atlantic and
Pacific sectors of the STZ. These regions are adjacent to the Southern Ocean’s winter
deep mixing band, where nutrient-rich waters are entrained into the euphotic zone. We
added supporting references (e.g., Rigby et al., 2020) to show that nutrient supply
increases are plausible in these regions during MCSs.
(3) Iron Supply in SAZ and AZ:
We have clarified that while deeper mixing during MCSs may supply some iron, the
effect is limited. In the AZ, deeper mixing also leads to reduced light availability and
enhanced sea ice formation, which scavenges dissolved iron (e.g., Lannuzel et al., 2007),
resulting in net iron removal. In the SAZ, while nitrate is abundant, iron remains the
primary limiting factor, and the modest deepening during MCSs is unlikely to deliver
sufficient iron from subsurface reservoirs.
(4) Division Rate vs. Biomass Accumulation
We thank the reviewer for this important distinction. The revised text now clearly
separates division rates (influenced by nutrient and light availability) and net biomass
change (the satellite-observed signal, governed by the balance between growth and loss
processes (e.g., grazing, sinking)). We now state that “the observed biomass anomalies
reflect net outcomes of phytoplankton division and loss rates,” aligning with the
framework proposed by Behrenfeld (2014) and others.

Lannuzel D, Schoemann V, de Jong J, Tison J-L, Chou L. Distribution and
biogeochemical behaviour of iron in the East Antarctic sea ice. Marine Chemistry 2007,
106(1-2): 18-32.
Richaud B, Hu X, Darmaraki S, Fennel K, Lu Y, Oliver ECJ. Drivers of Marine
Heatwaves in the Arctic Ocean. Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans 2024, 129(2).
Behrenfeld MJ. Climate-mediated dance of the plankton. Nature Climate Change 2014,
4(10): 880-887.
