criterion and has become widely adopted in the literature to ensure consistency and
facilitate inter-study comparisons. Extending the baseline to include more recent years

ocean warming, potentially leading to a shifting baseline and an underestimation of the

comparability with previous studies, we therefore retained the fixed 1982–2011
climatological period in our analysis. This rationale has been clarified in the revised
Methods section.

Response to Reviewer #2
(Note: Reviewer comments in black and our point-to-point replies in blue)
The current manuscript describes results from an analysis of satellite data regarding
impacts of extreme events (heat waves & cold spells) in the Southern Ocean. The
analysis reveals some interesting patterns and temporal trends, but there are major
weakness that compromise the integrity of the work and the robustness of the
conclusions. Below are specific comments beginning with major issues and followed
by minor comments.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful evaluation of our manuscript and
for highlighting both the strengths and areas requiring improvement. We appreciate
your acknowledgment of the novel spatial and temporal patterns identified in our
analysis. At the same time, we take seriously your concerns regarding the
methodological rigor and robustness of the conclusions. In response, we have carefully
addressed each of your specific comments and have made substantial revisions to the
manuscript to enhance its scientific integrity, clarity, and overall impact. These changes
include refining the methodological descriptions, improving dataset consistency,
clarifying the use of region-specific algorithms, strengthening model validation,
and updating our interpretation of key results. We believe these revisions have significantly
improved the quality and robustness of the study. A detailed point-by-point response to
each of your comments follows below.
Major Issues
1) All analyses regarding phytoplankton size classes and size distributions reported in
this study are not robust. The primary issue is that the authors are using global
relationships from previous publications and applying them to interpretations of
anomalies. For example, the phytoplankton size structure model of Sun et al. (2023) is
based on a global field data set (see their figure 1) where model performance is
evaluated over property values spanning multiple orders of magnitude (see their figure
3). It is clear in their figure 3 that even when plotted on log-log axes, there is significant
unexplained variance. If this model is then applied to Southern Ocean only data for
relatively small anomalies in SST and chlorophyll, there is no reason to believe that the
modeled predictions in phytoplankton size classes are robust. A similar issue also holds
for the Waga et al. (2019) model on phytoplankton size structure (or what the current
authors refer to as the chlorophyll size distribution, CSD). The Waga et al. paper is
focused on the impact of mesoscale eddies on CSD and is not inherently equally valid
for large scale impacts of extreme events. Waga et al. evaluated their model
performance based on, primarily, northern hemisphere data on the western edge of the
pacific ocean (see their figure 1), with limited data from the Southern Ocean with
undefined seasonal representation (and with roughly half of the data collected
immediately next to the Antarctic continent). The model used information on both
chlorophyll and spectral absorption, with the latter property included to aid in
retrievals in oligotrophic waters (essentially irrelevant for the current analysis. Waga et al.’s
resultant model was validated by comparing in situ CSD slopes to predicted slopes for
a dynamic range in values from ~0.5 to 3 (see their figure 2), an analysis the exhibited
significant unexplained variance. For the current study, reported anomalies in CSDs
associated with extreme events appear to largely fall within the range of +/- 0.1, which
certainly can not be considered significant (or even robust in sign) given the Waga et al
evaluation of model performance. Given the above considerations, I do not believe the
evaluation of community composition impacts of extreme events presented in the current
manuscript are robust and recommend that these be removed in future versions of this paper.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this critical and thoughtful assessment. We fully
acknowledge the concern regarding the limitations of applying globally derived
models—particularly those with substantial unexplained variance—to evaluate
relatively small anomalies in phytoplankton size structure, especially in a region as
optically and ecologically unique as the Southern Ocean. To address your concerns, we
have removed all analyses and results related to the chlorophyll size distribution (CSD)
model (Waga et al., 2019) from the manuscript. We agree that, given the limited
Southern Ocean validation and the narrow range of observed CSD anomalies (±0.1),
this metric does not provide a robust or interpretable signal in the context of extreme
events. Regarding the PSC model, we retained the PSC model of Sun et al. (2023) in
the revised manuscript, with important caveats and enhancements. We agree that the
original model was trained on global datasets and its application to Southern Ocean
anomalies requires validation. To this end, we conducted an independent evaluation
using a large in situ HPLC dataset (n = 3508 samples) from the Southern Ocean
spanning 1998–2023. Our analysis shows good agreement between model-predicted
and pigment-derived size class fractions (see revised Supplementary Figures 3 and 4),
indicating that the PSC model captures the dominant spatial and seasonal patterns of
phytoplankton community structure in this region. While we recognize that the PSC
model does not explicitly resolve short-term ecological dynamics such as grazing,
mixing history, or physiological acclimation, it provides a first-order estimate of
community shifts based on Chl-a and SST anomalies. We have now clarified these
limitations in the Discussion and Methods sections, and we emphasize that our
interpretations are qualitative and pattern-oriented rather than absolute.
2) (lines 182-236) I found this discussion of mechanisms for phytoplankton responses
inconsistent and not adequately supported. Here are specific examples:
a. (line 189-191) Here it is stated that phytoplankton in the SAZ are iron limited, but
then it says that MHWs alleviate light limitation and stimulate growth. First issue is
that there is no evidence provided that MHWs alleviate light limitation. Second, there
is no connection made between an increase in light and how that stimulates iron limited
phytoplankton.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that the original explanation
was incomplete and insufficiently supported. In the revised manuscript, we have
substantially rewritten this section to clarify the proposed mechanism:
(1) Light availability during MHWs. We now explicitly state that marine heatwaves
tend to enhance stratification and shoal the mixed layer, which increases the average
light exposure for phytoplankton—particularly in high-latitude regions where deep
mixing often limits irradiance.
(2) Interaction with iron limitation. We have clarified that MHWs alone do not directly
alleviate iron limitation in the SAZ. However, in regions with episodic or background
iron enrichment (e.g., via upwelling or dust deposition), the combination of increased
light and partial iron availability may support enhanced phytoplankton growth. We have
removed any implication of a direct causal link between MHWs and iron supply, and
instead frame the response as context-dependent.
b. (lines 191 -195) Here is it stated that in the AZ phytoplankton are co-limited by iron
and light, but no evidence is provided that this is always the case. More likely, the cells
are limited by light only in winter months, noting here that many MHWs for the AZ
occur in fall and winter (figure 1g). It is then stated that MHWs enhance water column
stability (no evidence provided), alleviate light limitation (no evidence provided), and
accelerate ice melt (no evidence provided), the latter alleviating iron stress (but
wouldn’t this only be immediately adjacent to melting ice?). So apparently the
suggestion in ‘a’ above about increased light alleviating iron stress was not based on
the presumption of changes in cellular stoichiometries for Fe.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for these insightful points. In the revised manuscript, we
have restructured this section to present a more nuanced, evidence-based discussion of
co-limitation and physical drivers in the Antarctic Zone. Specifically:
(1) Seasonal variability of limitation regimes
We agree that light limitation is more pronounced in winter and early spring, while co-
limitation by light and iron typically emerges during the growing season. We have
clarified that our analysis focuses on biologically active periods—when MHWs
intersect with phytoplankton growth potential (i.e., austral spring to autumn)—and not
on the full annual cycle. We now explicitly note that light limitation dominates in winter
and that MHWs occurring during non-productive months are unlikely to yield
significant biological responses.
(2) Mechanisms supporting enhanced phytoplankton growth during MHWs
 Water column stability: We now reference Hayashida et al. (2020) and Sun et al.
(2024), who show that MHWs are often accompanied by stronger stratification and
reduced mixed layer depth, particularly in the Antarctic Zone.
 Alleviation of light limitation: We cite Doney et al. (2006), who reported that
shallower mixed layers associated with warming events increased mean irradiance
exposure for phytoplankton in the euphotic zone.
 Sea ice melt and iron supply: We have revised this explanation to emphasize that
relief from iron limitation due to MHW-induced sea ice melt is strongest near the
ice edge (Richaud et al., 2024). However, we also note that iron-rich meltwater can
be advected over mesoscale distances and influence productivity in broader regions,
as supported by Loscher et al. (1997), De Baar et al. (2001), and Lannuzel et al.
(2007).
(3) Clarification of mechanism
We confirm that our explanation does not rely on changes in cellular Fe stoichiometry.
Rather, we describe how MHW-driven environmental changes may simultaneously
mitigate light and iron constraints—through physical processes—thereby facilitating a
more favorable environment for phytoplankton growth in regions that are typically co-
limited.
c. (line 197-199) Here it is stated that enhanced mixing in the STZ (no evidence
provided) alleviates nitrate limitation and promotes phytoplankton growth. First, the
assumption here is that the increase in chlorophyll in the STZ during MCS is due to an
increase in biomass. IF the supposition is correct that the mixed layer deepens during
an MCS, how do the authors know that the change in chlorophyll isn’t simply
photoacclimation to lower average mixed layer light levels? If it is an increase in
nutrient supply, one would have to show that the increase in mixing depth was sufficient
to penetrate the nutricline, otherwise there is no strong reason to think that the deeper
mixing (how much deeper, by the way, a few meters, tens of meters?) impacted nutrient
supply. Second, it is then stated that the deeper mixing during MCS in the SAZ and AZ
caused greater light limitation. But it was stated prior to this that these regions are also
iron limited (actually, during summer months they are iron limited more than light
limited, as in situ iron fertilization experiments have shown). No explanation is
provided why deeper mixing in the SAZ and AZ doesn’t also increase iron supply to
the mixed layer. Finally, be careful with the word ‘growth’. Do you mean cell division
rates or changes in biomass. The two are not the same. The mechanisms you discuss
are relevant to division rate, but what you observed from space are changes in biomass,
which are also controlled by loss processes (which are barely mentioned at all in this
manuscript).
Reply: We appreciate this detailed and insightful comment. In the revised manuscript,
we have significantly restructured this section to address these key concerns. Below we
summarize the main clarifications and revisions made:
(1) Biomass vs. Photoacclimation
We agree that observed increases in surface Chl-a could reflect changes in biomass,
cellular pigmentation, or both. To address this:
(a) We now include an analysis of satellite-derived particulate backscatter (bbp(443))
to estimate phytoplankton carbon, which supports biomass increases during MCSs (see
Extended Data Fig. 4).
(b) We explicitly note that changes in the Chl-a:carbon ratio (θ) indicate contributions
from both biomass and photoacclimation.
(c) The revised text avoids assuming a direct translation from Chl-a to biomass and
acknowledges physiological responses as a possible factor.
(2) MLD Deepening and Nutricline Penetration
We now cite GLORYS12V1 reanalysis data showing that during MCSs, the MLD
increased by an average of 4.25 ± 0.92 m globally, and by 20–30 m in the Atlantic and
Pacific sectors of the STZ. These regions are adjacent to the Southern Ocean’s winter
deep mixing band, where nutrient-rich waters are entrained into the euphotic zone. We
added supporting references (e.g., Rigby et al., 2020) to show that nutrient supply
increases are plausible in these regions during MCSs.
(3) Iron Supply in SAZ and AZ:
We have clarified that while deeper mixing during MCSs may supply some iron, the
effect is limited. In the AZ, deeper mixing also leads to reduced light availability and
enhanced sea ice formation, which scavenges dissolved iron (e.g., Lannuzel et al., 2007),
resulting in net iron removal. In the SAZ, while nitrate is abundant, iron remains the
primary limiting factor, and the modest deepening during MCSs is unlikely to deliver
sufficient iron from subsurface reservoirs.
(4) Division Rate vs. Biomass Accumulation
We thank the reviewer for this important distinction. The revised text now clearly
separates division rates (influenced by nutrient and light availability) and net biomass
change (the satellite-observed signal, governed by the balance between growth and loss
processes (e.g., grazing, sinking)). We now state that “the observed biomass anomalies
reflect net outcomes of phytoplankton division and loss rates,” aligning with the
framework proposed by Behrenfeld (2014) and others.

Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. We have removed this part in the revised

Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We agree that the term “massive”

have removed this term in the revised manuscript to ensure the language more

Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. We have removed this part in the revised

g. (lines 205-206) Here the authors invoke temperature limitation. How does this play

Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that SST
anomalies during MHWs and MCSs in the Southern Ocean are typically modest—
generally <2 °C, as shown in Figure 3—and that such small changes may not directly
constrain or enhance phytoplankton division rates in isolation. As noted in previous
studies (e.g., Arrigo et al., 2012; Vehmaa & Salonen, 2009), phytoplankton blooms can
occur even in near-freezing waters, and low temperatures do not necessarily inhibit
biomass accumulation. Furthermore, temperature changes of this magnitude are often
less influential than concurrent shifts in iron availability, light exposure, and grazing
pressure. For example, reduced temperatures during MCSs may indirectly favor net
biomass accumulation by lowering zooplankton grazing rates (López-Urrutia, 2008;
Taucher & Oschlies, 2011), while deeper mixing may enhance nutrient supply
irrespective of thermal effects. In light of this, we have removed the reference to
temperature limitation as a primary control and revised the discussion to focus on the
interaction of temperature with physical and ecological processes, rather than invoking
direct thermal limitation of growth. We appreciate the reviewer’s comment, which
helped us clarify and strengthen this part of the manuscript.
h. (lines 207-209) Here it is stated that MCSs in the AZ promote sea ice formation and
this absorbs dissolved iron. What evidence do you have that sea ice formation changed
significantly during the MCSs? If it did increase, these areas of sea ice formation would
not provide valid satellite chlorophyll retrievals would they? I’m also not aware of ice
formation drawing iron out of surrounding waters, only trapping the iron in the water
that is being frozen, so I don’t see how sea ice formation would significantly impact
iron levels away from the sea ice (i.e., in the waters where you get satellite chlorophyll
data).
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. We agree that the link
between sea ice formation and iron dynamics is nuanced and that direct observational
evidence of MCS-induced changes in iron availability is limited—particularly in
satellite-accessible, ice-free regions. Our original statement aimed to present a
hypothesized mechanism rather than a confirmed effect. In the revised manuscript, we
now clarify the following:
(1) Sea ice formation and iron sequestration
During ice formation, dissolved iron can become trapped within the forming sea ice
matrix (De Baar et al., 2001; Lannuzel et al., 2007). This process reduces the
availability of iron in the surrounding water column, but primarily within the immediate
zone of ice formation.
(2) Limitations of satellite observations
We acknowledge that satellite-derived chlorophyll-a cannot be retrieved in ice-covered
waters. Therefore, any influence of sea ice formation on iron availability and
phytoplankton would be indirect—possibly affecting adjacent open-water regions
through changes in surface mixing or lateral advection, but this cannot be resolved
directly with the available data.
(3) Revision for clarity
We have revised the manuscript to explicitly describe this as a speculative mechanism,
framed within the broader discussion of factors potentially contributing to suppressed
phytoplankton responses during MCSs in the AZ. We no longer present this as a
definitive explanation and have removed language that could imply direct causality.

Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important observation. We agree that the

Where is the evidence that this is significant? Iron enrichment experiments indicate that

Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important point. We agree that introducing silicate

k.(lines 224-236) In this paragraph, the message has gotten completely confused with

Response to Reviewer #3
(Note: Reviewer comments in black and our point-to-point replies in blue)
Key Results
The authors investigate the response of phytoplankton size structures in the Southern
Ocean during marine heat waves (MHW) and marine cold spells (MCS) using a suite
of satellite-based data and modelling approaches. Their results showed MHWs were
most frequent in the Subtropics and Subantarctic. Contrasting this, they found that
MCSs were more frequent in the Antarctic Zone. Some of the results section on the
response of phytoplankton (and their size classes) to MHWs and MCSs were difficult
to follow - I have highlighted some examples below in the section on clarity. The
authors show that during MCSs in the Subtropical Zone, picoplankton increased
whereas in the Antarctic and Subantarctic Zone micro and nano plankton decreased.
They also show that the inverse was true for MHW, with micro and nano size classes
increasing in the Antarctic Zone. I think that it is an excellent idea to study the effects
of MHWs and MCSs on phytoplankton in the Southern Ocean. However, the methods
and data used in this study are not reproducible, and the choice of data products is not
detailed, and in some cases poorly chosen. As such I cannot recommend this article for
publication and suggest that this article is not accepted. Below, I have detailed my
reasoning, and I hope that the authors find my feedback helpful and constructive. If the
authors choose to resumbit the paper, I strongly suggest that they vigorously consider
and scrutinise their choice of data and methods.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback.
We fully acknowledge the concerns raised regarding methodological clarity, data
product selection, and result interpretation. In response, we have undertaken a
comprehensive revision of the manuscript. Major changes include:
(1) Substantial restructuring of the Results section to improve clarity and flow.
(2) Replacement of previously used data products with those more appropriate for
Southern Ocean conditions, such as regionally validated chlorophyll-a algorithms and
PSC-based phytoplankton size estimation.
(3) Removal of less robust analyses (e.g., the CSD slope model) and addition of
validation using in situ data where available.
(4) Clearer description of methods and data sources to ensure reproducibility, now
detailed in both the main text and Supplementary Information.
We have also refined the Discussion to ensure that interpretations are well-supported
and more cautiously framed. Figures have been updated accordingly to reflect these
improvements. We hope these substantial revisions address the reviewer’s concerns and
improve the scientific rigor and clarity of the manuscript.
Validity
Based on the figures provided, I believe that the interpretations of these results support
the trends of phytoplankton size classes during MHW and MCS events. However, I
think that their discussion on the biogeochemical / environment drivers underpinning
these changes requires further work. There is no mention of phytoplankton groups or
taxonomy. For example, in the Subantarctic Zone haptophytes (E. hux) dominate (Balch et al., 2014). It is widely recognised that in the Antarctic Zone diatoms and haptophyes (P. antarctica) are dominant (Smith et al., 2014; Hayward et al., 2024). These different groups, and species within them, respond differently to environmental stimuli. As such, the discussion on phytoplankton size classes should be accompanied by discussing phytoplankton speciation and phenology.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that taxonomic
composition plays a key role in shaping regional phytoplankton responses and that
species-level differences are critical for interpreting size-based trends. In the revised
Discussion, we have included additional context referencing the dominant taxa in each
zone—such as Emiliania huxleyi in the Subantarctic Zone and diatoms and Phaeocystis
antarctica in the Antarctic Zone (Balch et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2014; Hayward et al.,
2024)—and have noted how their differing ecophysiological traits may contribute to
the observed patterns in size structure during MHW and MCS events. We also clarify
the limitations of our approach: the PSC algorithm used in this study estimates size
class composition but cannot resolve species or functional group taxonomy. We now
explicitly acknowledge this constraint and highlight that integrating satellite data with
in situ taxonomic observations and functional trait modeling represents an important
avenue for future work.
Significance
I think that these results would be significant and important to biogeochemists,
ecosystem modellers and earth system scientists. However, I struggle to move past the
poorly detailed methods and data used in the study.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the broader relevance of our
findings and acknowledge the concern regarding insufficient methodological detail. In
response, we have thoroughly revised the Methods section to improve transparency and
reproducibility. Key updates include:
(1) Explicit identification and justification of all data products used;
(2) Clear definitions of MHW and MCS criteria;
(3) Detailed descriptions of anomaly calculations, temporal smoothing, and spatial
gridding;
(4) An expanded explanation of the PSC-based size class estimation and associated
validation steps.
Data and methodology
The methods and data used in this manuscript lack scientific rigour and are not
reproducible. This is primarily the reason I am not accepting this article. I have detailed
my reasoning thoroughly below. The data used in the study would benefit from clearer
definition and more detailed justification to ensure it is well-suited to the study's
objectives. For chlorophyll a (Chl-a) data the authors state that they used ‘chlorophyll
from CMEMS’. A CMEMS database search showed there are 54 different Chl-a
products available on CMEMS. See Pauthenet et al., (2024) which details differences
in commonly used Chl-a products. It is very important to specify what product is used
to ensure results are reproducible, but to also further understand potential uncertainties
and biases. The authors should state what CMEMS product was chosen and why it was
used in the study. Furthermore, it has not been possible to assess any code as in the
‘code availability’ statement, all the authors said was that the analysis was conducted
in Matlab.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for highlighting these important issues. In the revised

(1) Chlorophyll-a Product Specification and Justification

rs
Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI v6.0, https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00281).
This product was selected for its long-term consistency and its improved performance

Southern Ocean, to estimate surface chlorophyll-a concentrations. The rationale for this
choice and its advantages over other products are now clearly explained.
(2) Improved Reproducibility and Code Availability:

Code Availability section, we now state that all scripts used in this study, written in

Additionally, key code components for processing chlorophyll-a, computing

(1998 - 2022). Furthermore, in 2019 MODIS-Aqua drifted out of orbit. There is

(1998–2022) and to address concerns related to post-2019 MODIS-Aqua data quality,
we now use daily R from the ESA Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI
rs
v6.0), which provides a consistent multi-sensor merged product with rigorous inter-
sensor calibration and gap-filling. We then apply a Southern Ocean–specific
chlorophyll-a algorithm to this OC-CCI Rrs dataset, enhancing both the temporal
continuity and the accuracy of chlorophyll estimates. This change ensures that our
phytoplankton size class estimates—derived using the PSC model—are based on a
higher-quality and longer-term dataset. We have revised the Methods section to reflect

The authors use the OISSTv2 product in their study to assess MHW and MCS. This
product is one of the older products used in SST remote sensing and no longer
considered the ‘gold standard’ (instead, see the SST CCI). The product is also of coarse
spatial resolution (.25 degrees) compared to more modern products, and does not match
the spatial resolution of chlorophyll data (4km). The authors interpolated the chl-a
product to make it coarser and on the same grid as the OISST product. In doing so they
will miss out on many of the finer scale processes in the dataset. One of the largest
caveats of this study is that the remote sensing of sea surface temperatures is not
possible for much of the year in polar regions due to ice cover. Where there is sea ice
the OISST algorithm estimates the under ice SST by a linear fit capped at -1.8 celsius.
As such, the MCSs observed in this study are not the result of actual satellite
observations, but could in fact be due to how the OISST product handles under ice
temperatures.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed feedback. In the revised manuscript, we
addressed these concerns as follows:
(1) Updated SST Product:
We replaced the OISSTv2 dataset with the more advanced ESA Sea Surface
Temperature Climate Change Initiative (ESA SST CCI v3.0) reanalysis product, which
provides improved accuracy, inter-sensor consistency, and bias correction suitable for
long-term climate analyses in polar regions.
(2) Sea Ice Considerations:
To mitigate the limitations of SST retrieval under ice cover, we applied a mask to
exclude regions with an annual average sea ice concentration (SIC) greater than 20%.
This reduces the likelihood of including SST anomalies that are artifacts of the under-
ice estimation algorithm used in SST datasets (as noted by the reviewer).
(3) Spatial Resolution Harmonization:
While we acknowledge that regridding the high-resolution chlorophyll-a product (OC-
CCI, native 4 km) to 0.25° resolution may reduce sensitivity to submesoscale variability,
we opted for this approach to maintain consistency across all parameters analyzed
(including SST, nutrients, and MLD). This facilitates robust spatial alignment in the
detection and attribution of MHW/MCS events and their ecological impacts. We have
now explicitly stated this limitation in the revised Methods and Discussion sections.
These updates ensure higher data fidelity and improve the robustness of our conclusions
regarding phytoplankton responses to thermal extremes in the Southern Ocean.
The methods section is very short, and there is no information provided on the CSD
model, other than a short description in the supplementary information. The PSC model
used was recently published (2023); and the PSC model is dependent on SST
observations. There should be discussion regarding uncertainty model uncertainty and
performance, especially when there can be issues of circularity as both the size class

MCSs.
Reply: Thank you for this important comment. In the revised manuscript, we have fully
removed the CSD model and associated analyses to improve methodological clarity and
focus. Regarding the PSC model (Sun et al., 2023), we acknowledge that it uses SST
as one of its key input variables. To address concerns about potential circularity—where
SST is used both to define MHW/MCS events and as a driver of phytoplankton size
class estimates—we took the following steps:
(1) Independent Validation:
We validated the PSC-derived phytoplankton size class outputs against in situ
observations from the Southern Ocean (1998–2023), which demonstrated good
agreement (details provided in the revised Methods and Supplementary Figures).
(2) Clarified Use of SST:
While SST is used in both MHW/MCS classification and as an input to the PSC model,
these serve distinct functions: (i) in the former, SST is used to define the timing and
intensity of thermal anomalies; (ii) in the latter, SST is used as an ecophysiological
proxy influencing phytoplankton size structure. We now explicitly acknowledge this
dual role in the Discussion, and we clarify that our analyses focus on relative anomalies
in size structure during MHWs and MCSs, rather than directly correlating SST with
size class output.
(3) Model Justification:
Previous studies (e.g., Sun et al., 2023; Moore et al., 2020) have shown that
phytoplankton size composition may vary substantially under environmental stress
even when total chlorophyll-a remains unchanged. SST has proven effective in
detecting these shifts in ecological niches. Thus, the PSC model remains a valuable tool
for interpreting community-scale responses to thermal extremes.
These clarifications and validations are now fully incorporated into the revised Methods
and Discussion sections.
Finally, there is inconsistency in the date ranges. Chl-a observations are only available

adding further inconsistencies.
Reply: Thank you for this insightful comment. We acknowledge that satellite-derived
chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) observations in high-latitude regions are seasonally limited,
primarily due to ice cover and reduced daylight during winter months. To minimize the
influence of inconsistent data coverage, we implemented the following measures in the
revised manuscript:
(1) Sea Ice Masking:
We applied a conservative mask to exclude regions with an annual average sea ice
concentration greater than 20%, thereby focusing our analysis on open-water areas
where satellite Chl-a retrievals are consistently valid.
(2) Aligned Time Windows:
While the SST dataset spans 1982–2023, the Chl-a dataset covers 1998–2023. To ensure
consistency, all analyses involving phytoplankton responses to MHWs and MCSs were
restricted to events occurring between 1998 and 2023—the common period for both
SST and Chl-a datasets.
(3) Climatology Construction:
Daily climatologies for both SST and Chl-a were constructed independently using their
respective time windows. Although their baseline periods differ (SST: 1982–2011; Chl-
a: 1998–2023), all anomaly analyses were constrained within the Chl-a observation
period, ensuring internal consistency in the biological response evaluations.
These steps ensure that our comparisons are methodologically sound and that observed
phytoplankton responses are not biased by inconsistent temporal coverage. This
clarification has been included in the revised Methods and Discussion sections.
